fig02_diverging_lines.title: Figure 2, The Dream Index
fig02_diverging_lines.what_you_see: Two lines tracking the cost of a canonical middle-class life and median household income in real 2024 dollars, 1960 to 2024.
fig02_diverging_lines.how_to_use: Scroll down beside the chart. Each scroll step adds one layer of the argument: first the income line, then the basket, then the era bands, then the crossing point.
fig02_diverging_lines.what_to_look_for: The moment in 2011 when the amber basket line crosses above the grey income line. Before 2011, the basket was cheaper. Since, it has been more expensive.
fig02_diverging_lines.source: FRED MEHOINUSA672N; project Dream Index methodology.

fig02_crossing.title: Figure 2 (Detail), The Crossing
fig02_crossing.what_you_see: A zoomed view of the same two lines, 2000 to 2024. The annotations mark three specific moments: the 2008 financial crisis, the 2011 crossing, and the 2022 rate floor end.
fig02_crossing.how_to_use: Hover any year for the basket cost and median income at that moment. The shaded rust area is the gap.
fig02_crossing.what_to_look_for: The brief period 2012 to 2021 when cheap mortgages disguised the structural problem, and the abrupt widening after 2022.

fig03_bifurcation.title: Figure 3, The Bifurcation
fig03_bifurcation.what_you_see: Real-dollar price changes for each component of American life, 1960 to 2024. Some categories fell, some rose.
fig03_bifurcation.how_to_use: Each bar is a single product or service. Compare what got cheaper (clothing, electronics) to what got more expensive (housing, healthcare, education).
fig03_bifurcation.what_to_look_for: The pattern of what cheapens: anything that can be imported or automated. The pattern of what rises: anything that requires human time and labor in a specific place.
fig03_bifurcation.source: BLS CPI series by category, 1960 to 2024.

fig07b_basket_composition.title: Figure 4, Composition of the basket
fig07b_basket_composition.what_you_see: A stacked area chart showing the six components of the Dream Basket as a share of total cost, 1960 to 2024. Click any legend item to toggle that component.
fig07b_basket_composition.how_to_use: Hover the stack at any year to read each component's share. Toggle items in the right-side legend to isolate a category.
fig07b_basket_composition.what_to_look_for: Healthcare's share grew from 5.5% to 25.3% of the basket. Housing's share shrank in percentage terms even as its real cost climbed, because the other categories grew faster.
fig07b_basket_composition.source: BLS CPI components; KFF, NCES; project basket methodology.

fig04_five_places.title: Figure 11, Five Americas
fig04_five_places.what_you_see: Median household income trajectories for five specific American communities, 1960 to 2024, each scaled to the national median (1.0).
fig04_five_places.how_to_use: Each line is one community. Above 1.0 is above national median. Below is behind.
fig04_five_places.what_to_look_for: How early each community's economic trajectory diverged from the national one. Pine Ridge has never been at 1.0. Coal Country fell after 1980. The Bay Area accelerated after 2000.
fig04_five_places.source: U.S. Census Bureau, IPUMS NHGIS aggregated to county, 1960 to 2020.

fig04b_community_abandonment.title: Figure 12, Mahoning County
fig04b_community_abandonment.what_you_see: Population and median income trajectories for Mahoning County, Ohio, 1960 to 2020, the heart of the Rust Belt collapse.
fig04b_community_abandonment.how_to_use: The vertical line marks Youngstown Black Monday, September 19, 1977.
fig04b_community_abandonment.what_to_look_for: How the population and the income decline simultaneously after 1977. When the plants closed, the people followed.
fig04b_community_abandonment.source: U.S. Census Bureau decennial census, 1960 to 2020.

fig05_wages_productivity.title: Figure 5, Wages vs. Productivity
fig05_wages_productivity.what_you_see: Two lines, both indexed to 1960 = 100. One tracks American productivity. The other tracks median hourly wages.
fig05_wages_productivity.how_to_use: Compare the slopes. Until 1973 they moved together. After 1973 they diverged.
fig05_wages_productivity.what_to_look_for: Productivity is now 3.5x its 1960 level, while wages are only 1.2x. The gap is where the asset contract begins.

fig06_income_wealth_race.title: Figure 13, Income vs. Wealth by Race
fig06_income_wealth_race.what_you_see: Two side-by-side comparisons. Black household income relative to white income (left), and Black household wealth relative to white wealth (right).
fig06_income_wealth_race.how_to_use: Compare the rates of change between the two panels.
fig06_income_wealth_race.what_to_look_for: Income gap narrowed by six points in 57 years. Wealth gap barely moved. The asset contract is the difference.
fig06_income_wealth_race.source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances; FRED.

fig06b_asset_compound.title: Figure 14, Compound the Difference
fig06b_asset_compound.what_you_see: An interactive calculator that compounds an income gap into a wealth gap over decades, at user-chosen returns and time horizons.
fig06b_asset_compound.how_to_use: Adjust the inputs (income gap, annual return, years) to see how a small wage difference compounds into a structural wealth difference.
fig06b_asset_compound.what_to_look_for: How quickly even a modest, sustained income gap becomes a wealth gap many times larger when the income holder cannot also accumulate appreciating assets.
fig06b_asset_compound.source: Synthesis using historical S&P 500 returns; SCF wealth distributions.

fig07_hours_of_work.title: Figure 6, Hours of work
fig07_hours_of_work.what_you_see: What forty hours of work could buy in 1960, versus forty hours in 2024. Same hours, different purchasing power.
fig07_hours_of_work.how_to_use: Each colored block within the bar represents one category of expense. Block width equals hours of work required.
fig07_hours_of_work.what_to_look_for: The blank space at the end of the 1960 week (purchasing power left over). The overflow in the 2024 week.
fig07_hours_of_work.source: BLS CPI; FRED median hourly wage.

fig_wealth_share.title: Figure 7, Where the gains went
fig_wealth_share.what_you_see: For every $100 of new wealth generated in the American economy between 1980 and 2024, this shows where each dollar landed.
fig_wealth_share.how_to_use: Each currency stack represents the share captured by that group.
fig_wealth_share.what_to_look_for: The top 1% captured $34 of every $100. The bottom 50% lost $2 in real terms.
fig_wealth_share.source: World Inequality Database (WID.world); Federal Reserve SCF.

fig_women_workforce.title: Figure 8, Women and the Dream
fig_women_workforce.what_you_see: Women's labor force participation 1960 to 2024, alongside the Dream Index trajectory.
fig_women_workforce.how_to_use: Compare the rise of women's workforce entry to the rise of the basket cost.
fig_women_workforce.what_to_look_for: The correlation between when the single-income household became unaffordable and when the dual-income household became the norm.

fig_immigrant_trajectories.title: Figure 9, Immigrant Economic Trajectories
fig_immigrant_trajectories.what_you_see: Median household income and homeownership for immigrant households, organized by decade of arrival.
fig_immigrant_trajectories.how_to_use: Each bar represents one arrival cohort. Pre-2000 arrivals (green) succeeded. Post-2010 (rust) face the post-crossing basket.
fig_immigrant_trajectories.source: U.S. Census ACS; Pew Research Center; NBER immigrant assimilation studies.

fig01_five_mechanisms_map.title: Figure 10, Five Mechanisms map
fig01_five_mechanisms_map.what_you_see: A map locating the five communities documented in this chapter and the mechanism that drove each one's relationship to the asset contract.
fig01_five_mechanisms_map.how_to_use: Each marker is a place. Hover to read the mechanism summary.
fig01_five_mechanisms_map.what_to_look_for: How geography and mechanism interact: extraction, exclusion, deindustrialization, never-included, and capture each maps to a distinct place.

fig10_way_of_life.title: Figure 15, Way of Life
fig10_way_of_life.what_you_see: Four life-course indicators: age at first marriage, fertility rate, multigenerational households, and deaths of despair.
fig10_way_of_life.how_to_use: Click each tab to view a different indicator. Each tracks the same period, 1960 to 2024.
fig10_way_of_life.what_to_look_for: The acceleration of all four trends after 2010, within years of the Dream Index crossing 1.0.

fig09_time_machine.title: Figure 16, Your Life on the Dream Index
fig09_time_machine.what_you_see: An interactive calculator that places your circumstances onto the Dream Index timeline.
fig09_time_machine.how_to_use: Enter your inputs. The Dream Index recalculates for your cohort and your community.
fig09_time_machine.what_to_look_for: Where your trajectory sits in the larger picture, and which of the project's five mechanisms most directly shape your position.
fig09_time_machine.source: Synthesis using project basket methodology, ACS cohort data, BLS regional cost-of-living indices.

fig09_find_yourself.title: Figure 17, Find Yourself
fig09_find_yourself.what_you_see: A guided panel that asks you about your generation, education, household type, children, and community, then computes your position on the Dream Index.
fig09_find_yourself.how_to_use: Adjust each input. The output card updates immediately.
fig09_find_yourself.what_to_look_for: How small changes in your inputs (one more child, a different city) shift your basket cost and your class tier.
fig09_find_yourself.source: Project basket methodology with community-specific cost-of-living multipliers.

fig11_seven_findings.title: Figure 18, Seven findings, one story
fig11_seven_findings.what_you_see: A composite summary of the seven structural findings the project documents.
fig11_seven_findings.how_to_use: Read each finding in order. Each number is supported by the figures above.
fig11_seven_findings.what_to_look_for: The pattern that connects them: every finding describes a different facet of the same shift from labor to asset.

fig12_action_plan.title: Figure 19, Your Action Plan
fig12_action_plan.what_you_see: A personalized action plan generator that turns your inputs into a concrete set of recommendations across housing, healthcare, childcare, education, and assets.
fig12_action_plan.how_to_use: Fill in your details and press Generate plan. Scroll inside the iframe to read the full plan.
fig12_action_plan.what_to_look_for: Which mechanism most needs your attention, and which interventions move your trajectory the most.
fig12_action_plan.source: Synthesis using project methodology; mechanism-specific intervention research.
